article.para:
Siliko Core is a library that takes in math expressions, like 2 + 5 * 4 and calculates the result, 22. This tutorial will walk you through writing a simple program to translate an expression passed to the program on the command line to a value, and display it to the user. Such as this:
./tutorial "2 + 3 * 5" > 17
This tutorial assumes you can build with a library and write C code. If you need help building with the Siliko Core library, see Linking with Siliko Core.
To simplify things, Siliko Core includes a single header to include all of its public headers. So, to access Siliko Cores types and functions, you should #include this header.

The first thing you will need to do when using the Siliko Core library in your code is to create a SilikoEngine object. A SilikoEngine provides the function lookup table that Siliko Core uses to find the internal implementation of an operator, like +, or a function like sin. The SilikoEngineCreate function is responsible for making a SilikoEngine object, and it returns a pointer to the object.

Since SilikoEngine is designed to be customizable, a new SilikoEngine doesn’t include any in-language functions on its own. After you create a new SilikoEngine, you can use the function SilikoInstallOperations to add the in-language functions used to support Siliko Core’s built-in operators, such as +, - and d. You can use the SilikoInstallMathFunctions function to install Siliko Core’s built-in functions that provide access to functions from the C standard library’s math.h header, such as sin or abs.

This setup gets Siliko Core’s internal functions to work, but when you are done with it, you should clean up its resources to avoid a memory leak. To do this, call the SilikoEngineDestroy function on the SilikoEngine pointer.

With these bits of house-keeping taken care of, you can proceed to the more meaty use of the library. Siliko Core needs a source of input characters to parse. This is done with the SilikoInput type. Siliko Core includes a function, SilikoStringInputCreate that will make a new SilikoInput object using a simple C string as its input. Since argv[1] is a normal C string, it can be passed to SilikoStringInputCreate.

After you have your string input setup, you can pass it on to the infix parser with the SilikoParseInfix function. The infix parser will generate a syntax tree representing the expression you passed to it, and return a pointer to the root node of that tree.
You can then evaluate the syntax tree to get a result from it.

A SilikoValue represents a simple number produced by or passed to the Siliko Core library. It holds either an integer, a real number, or an error code. Because matters of user interface are left to the application, Siliko Core doesn’t include a facility to display the value. So, for this example, we will switch over the status, and print the resulting value, or an error message if the value is an error.

Some cleanup is needed for these objects, too. Because the infix parser consumes the SilikoInput, the parser also takes care of cleaning up the SilikoInput, so you do not need to clean up the SilikoInput, nor should you. The SilikoNode returned by SilikoParseInfix and the SilikoValue returned by SilikoEvaluate do need to be cleaned up. Siliko Core provides functions, SilikoNodeDestroy to clean up a SilikoNode and its branches, and SilikoValueDestroy to clean up a SilikoValue. Add these along with SilikoEngineDestroy.
